name: Gods, Heroes and Epics
description: Fifty whole stories, each told entire: every myth of a single deity, a hero's complete life, or one epic from its first line to its last, drawn from the Greek, Roman, Norse, Egyptian, Mesopotamian, Indian, Celtic, Japanese, Chinese, Mesoamerican, West African, Finnish, Persian and Central Asian cycles. Each subject carries twenty chapters that follow the story in order, written in a calm, even register for long listening, and each chapter says plainly which text, image or excavation it rests on.

exclusions: No invented episodes, invented quotations, invented dialogue, or invented details of a scene; tell only what a source contains and say plainly where the sources stop.
No claim that a myth is true or false; the subject is what a tradition tells and how it has been transmitted, never whether it happened.
No mockery, no debunking tone, and no framing of any tradition as primitive, superstitious, or lesser than any other on this list.
No living people are named, no living religious authority is characterised, and no living community is described or spoken for.
No third-party characters, franchises, brands, adaptations, films, games, or modern retellings; only the traditional and documented material.
No sensational treatment of violence, sexual assault, or mutilation in a myth: state what the source says in one plain sentence and give the consequence and the transmission the time instead.
No hooks, cliffhangers, teasers, questions to the listener, or promises about what is coming later, at the opening of a chapter or anywhere inside it.
No dates, provenances, or manuscript claims stated more precisely than the scholarship allows, and no source cited by title, author, or shelfmark.
Keep every chapter self-contained, resolving to a quiet close, with no reference forward to a later chapter and no callback to an earlier one.
No harmonising of variants into one smooth version: where two sources disagree, say so plainly and give both, without choosing between them.
prompt_context: Each episode tells one god, one hero or one epic entire, and each chapter is one stage of that story told from beginning to quiet end. Begin a chapter by naming what happens in it, plainly, in the first sentence; the chapter titles are the story in order, so a listener who wakes in the middle always knows where they are. Tell the tradition as the tradition tells it — the gods act, the hero travels, the object is made — without ever claiming or denying that any of it occurred, and without a single sentence that treats a tradition as quaint, primitive or mistaken. Every one of these cycles was somebody's religion and several still are; write as if a believer and a scholar were both listening, because both are. Say where each chapter comes from: the kind of text, the kind of image, the kind of excavation. Describe source types rather than naming a title, an author, or a shelfmark, and where two sources disagree, give both and leave the disagreement standing rather than smoothing it into one version. Real gods, heroes and historical figures are named plainly; nobody living is named, and no modern community is described or spoken for. Violence, mutilation and coercion appear in almost every one of these cycles; state what the source says in one plain sentence and then move to the consequence, the cult, the festival, the object or the transmission, which is where the interest actually is. This is a sleep compilation, so keep the tempo even and low the whole way through and let the detail carry it — the shape of an object, the plan of a sanctuary, the number of gates, the season of a festival, the difference between two manuscripts. Invent nothing. End each chapter on something still: a temple closed, a poem written down, a stone that is still shown, a name that survives in a landscape.

evidence_expectations: Ground each chapter in the kind of source named by the slot, and describe source types rather than citing any specific title, author, manuscript, or shelfmark.
Say in every chapter whether the episode rests on a text, on an image, on an excavation, or on a modern collector's field notes, and never let the four blur together.
Where an episode survives in two versions that disagree, give both and say they disagree, rather than choosing one or blending them.
Distinguish what a tradition says from what has been physically found, and say plainly when a site, an object or a route has been proposed but not established.
State the transmission honestly: how late the surviving manuscript is, whether the text was written by people who shared the beliefs, and what was lost.
Where a cycle is part of a living religion, say so plainly and describe present practice as present practice, without characterising anybody who holds it.
compatibility_rules: Pair only with the sleep history compilation formula; this pack assumes long, even chapters with no tension carried between them and no build across the episode.
Use one subject per episode and never mix two, so an episode is one god, one hero or one epic told whole rather than an anthology.
Draw the twenty slots of a subject in order rather than at random, because the slots are the story in sequence and shuffling them breaks the promise the episode makes.
Never reuse a slot within one episode set; each slot is one stage of one story and a repeat would tell the same stage twice.
Do not pair with any formula that opens on a hook, builds tension, promises a revelation, or ends a chapter pointing forward; the exclusions forbid all four and the material does not need them.
